candidateRows: Classical divine simplicity excludes several distinct forms of composition in God, including distinctions involving essence, attributes, action, existence, potency, and matter.
This taxonomy specifies the commitments under dispute and supplies the conceptual structure used by both speakers throughout their subsequent arguments.
After the general definition of divine simplicity, Joe develops a more precise account of the different compositions classical theists deny in God.
The disputed kinds of divine composition should be assessed individually, while recognizing that Aristotelian classical theism treats them as manifestations of act-potency composition.
The move provides the pro side's unifying metaphysical rationale for the preceding taxonomy and establishes how the separate disputes should be evaluated.
Joe's preceding taxonomy of the forms of composition excluded from God
Chris accepts most of Joe's taxonomy, qualifies the essence-existence formulation, and connects the distinctions through Aristotelian act and potency.
Divine simplicity does not identify creaturely knowledge with creaturely power; analogical predication allows one simple divine reality to resemble multiple distinct creaturely perfections.
This directly addresses an apparent contradiction in identifying God's attributes and supplies analogy as the pro side's principal coherence mechanism.
The moderator's objection that omniscience and omnipotence cannot be exactly the same property
In response to a challenge about identical divine attributes, Chris distinguishes analogical divine predication from univocal creaturely properties.
For purposes of absolute divine simplicity, a part can be understood as any positive ontological item intrinsic to a subject yet distinct from that subject.
The definition fixes the criterion by which alleged intrinsic distinctions count as composition, enabling the later objections to target a precise thesis.
Before presenting objections, Joe defines parts through positive ontological items, intrinsicness, and numerical distinction from their subject.
Divine simplicity denies real intrinsic distinctions in God but permits grounded conceptual distinctions and contingent extrinsic predications concerning creatures.
The qualifications delimit the doctrine's actual commitments and preserve room for meaningful divine attributes, relational changes, and contingent creature-directed predications.
Joe's formulation that anything intrinsic to God must be identical to God
Chris refines the proposed definition by distinguishing real identity from conceptual differentiation and intrinsic features from extrinsic relations.
Divine simplicity is motivated by divine aseity because intrinsic parts would make God's being or properties depend upon something that is not identical to God.
This is a principal positive argument for the doctrine, deriving the absence of divine composition from God's metaphysical ultimacy and radical independence.
Chris argues from God's status as the ultimate independent source of reality to the conclusion that God cannot depend upon intrinsic components.

Aseity need not require divine simplicity because dependence may be merely counterfactual, the whole may ground its parts, Trinitarian multiplicity may resist the strong requirement, or aseity may exclude only external dependence.
The move directly challenges the principal aseity argument through several alternative accounts of dependence, priority, Trinitarian structure, and divine independence.
Chris's argument that intrinsic parts would compromise God's complete metaphysical independence
Joe surveys four strategies by which a nonclassical theist might retain divine aseity without accepting the full doctrine of divine simplicity.

The relevant threat to aseity is explanatory grounding rather than mere counterfactual dependence, and priority monism fails because God cannot ground the unity that makes his alleged parts one being.
This defends the central aseity inference by sharpening the required dependence relation and identifying the unity of parts as the residual explanatory ground.
Joe's counterfactual-dependence distinction and priority-monist proposal that God grounds God's own parts
Chris concedes that bare counterfactual dependence is insufficient but argues that the unity of divine parts would still explain and ground the composite God.
Classical natural-theology arguments support divine simplicity because they terminate in a purely actual first cause, while every relevant kind of composition introduces potency.
This supplies an independent positive route to simplicity from pure actuality, connecting a prominent argument for God with the exclusion of composition.
Using Aquinas's first way as the main example, Chris argues that the unmoved mover's pure actuality rules out act-potency compositions in God.
Divine simplicity is best treated as a constellation of composition-specific debates, since each proposed kind of divine composition has multiple distinct arguments for and against it.
The framing governs how the motion should be analyzed by preventing arguments about one form of composition from being treated as decisive for every form.
As the discussion transitions into objections, Chris emphasizes that the doctrine encompasses multiple separable questions rather than one undifferentiated dispute.
Trinitarianism and classical divine simplicity form an inconsistent tetrad if eternal processions are positive ontological items intrinsic to but distinct from God.
This formulates the principal Trinitarian objection by identifying the exact incompatibility alleged between real processions, Trinitarian doctrine, and simplicity.
After introductory remarks about the debate's limited scope, Joe presents four jointly inconsistent claims and challenges the classical theist to identify which claim should be rejected.
A Latin Trinitarian model preserves simplicity by identifying each divine person and procession-relation with the divine essence while distinguishing persons through opposed relations.
This is the classical-theist's central reconciliation of divine simplicity with Trinitarian doctrine and directly rejects the objection's decisive premise.
Joe's claim that Trinitarian processions constitute positive intrinsic items distinct from God.

Chris concedes that social Trinitarian models conflict with simplicity but argues that a Latin model treats persons as the divine essence and distinguishes them relationally rather than compositionally.
Because the Son is begotten while God as such is not begotten, the Son appears strictly distinct from the Godhead and therefore an intrinsic constituent generating composition.
This presses an asymmetric relational difference against the proposed identity model and attempts to restore the Trinitarian composition objection after Chris's reply.
Chris's claim that persons and procession-relations are identical with the one divine essence.
After a side discussion about whether Trinitarian language is analogical, Joe returns to the dispute and argues from the asymmetry between the begotten Son and the unbegotten Godhead.
The Son is identical with his begottenness relationally and with the divine essence absolutely, while relational directedness adds no positive ontological item to God.
This directly answers the alleged begottenness-based distinction by explaining how relational opposition can distinguish persons without adding intrinsic composition.
Joe's contention that the Son's begottenness strictly distinguishes him from God as such.
Chris invokes the metaphysics of relations, distinguishing the Son considered relationally from the divine essence considered absolutely and denying that directedness is an additional entity.
The possible world in which God creates nothing makes contingent divine knowledge intrinsic to God, yielding a contingent intrinsic item or accident incompatible with divine simplicity.
The argument directly targets the coherence of simplicity, divine freedom, and omniscient knowledge of contingent truths in a creationless possible world.

Joe derives the possibility of God's existing alone from divine creative freedom, argues that nothing in that world could be extrinsic, and infers that God's contingent knowledge would be an accident.
Existing alone does not prevent God from having extrinsic properties, because God can lose aloneness merely through another thing's existence without any intrinsic change in God.
This attacks the crucial inference from a world containing only God to the intrinsicness of every property there, thereby challenging the aloneness argument's foundation.
Joe's premise that God cannot possess anything extrinsic in a possible world where only God exists.
Chris situates the objection against traditional accounts of immutable divine knowledge, then uses aloneness as a counterexample to the proposed test for intrinsic properties.
Knowledge is extrinsic even for a lone knower because its factive truth condition can change through external reality without any intrinsic change in the knowing subject.
This directly addresses contingent knowledge rather than properties generally and supplies an independent reason that divine knowledge can remain extrinsic in an alone world.
Joe's claim that contingent knowledge in the alone world must be wholly intrinsic to God.
Using a hypothetical lone human who knows there are no dogs, Chris argues that dogs could arise without changing the knower intrinsically while making the belief false and ending the knowledge.
The objection permits an extrinsic truth component while maintaining that contingent divine knowledge also has an intrinsic component contingently possessed by God.
This preserves the critic's knowledge-based objection against the claim that the extrinsic character of truth by itself dissolves the alleged conflict with simplicity.
Chris's claim that knowledge is extrinsic because its truth depends on realities external to the knower.
After Chris argues that all knowledge is extrinsic through factivity, Joe clarifies his premise, rejects aloneness as a property counterexample, and invokes contingent truthmakers.
If an immutable and purely actual God cannot gain or lose knowledge, yet changing contingent reality requires such epistemic change, then classical theism is false.
This is a direct act-potency and omniscience argument alleging that divine simplicity and immutability cannot accommodate knowledge of dynamically changing contingent reality.
Joe introduces a new act-potency objection, supports the immutability premise through classical-theist authorities, and derives changing divine knowledge from changing truths and omniscience.
The act-potency argument equivocates between knowledge as an intrinsic positive reality in God and knowledge as a partly extrinsic predication involving changing truths.
The distinction directly blocks the critic's inference to potentiality in God by locating changes in known contingent truths rather than in God's intrinsic reality.
Joe's argument that changing contingent truths require God to acquire and lose knowledge, thereby introducing potentiality into God.
Chris distinguishes predicables from real intrinsic properties, argues that truth is extrinsic, and explains changing knowledge attributions through changes in creatures rather than God.
An extremely extrinsic account of divine knowledge risks ceasing to describe knowledge unless it explains what God's changing knowledge actually consists in.
The challenge presses the pro account to supply an intelligible constitution of knowledge rather than merely redescribe temporal changes wholly outside God.
Chris's proposal that changing divine knowledge predications are explained by extrinsic changes in contingent reality without intrinsic change in God.
Using dinosaurs changing from actual to extinct, Joe asks what the corresponding divine knowledge consists in and questions whether the highly extrinsic model remains recognizable as knowledge.
God's contingent knowledge includes his intrinsic intellect and causal efficacy, while the difference between temporally varying knowledge attributions is entirely extrinsic.
This supplies the requested metaphysical account and preserves immutable divine simplicity while allowing true knowledge predications to vary with contingent temporal reality.
Joe's dinosaur-based challenge asking what changing divine knowledge consists in under an extrinsic model and whether it still counts as knowledge.
Chris concedes that divine knowledge is more extrinsic than creaturely knowledge, then grounds each item in God's intellect and causality while assigning their difference to creaturely history.
God could rationally choose an alone world because unknown reasons, undiluted perfection, or divine self-sufficiency may favor refraining from creation.
The possible rationality of an alone world supports the modal scenario used in the debate's arguments about divine freedom and contingent knowledge.
In response to an audience question about why God would ever be alone, Joe offers skeptical-theist and substantive reasons compatible with a voluntary absence of creatures.
God can exist alone because perfect goodness is already complete in him, making creation a gratuitous act for creatures rather than an improvement to God or reality.
The account connects divine self-sufficiency and freedom to the possibility of noncreation, reinforcing the modal coherence of classical theism's alone-world scenario.
Chris agrees that God may exist alone and argues that creation adds no perfection to God, instead expressing gratuitous grace toward creatures and ultimately divine glory.
Absolute distinctions among God's love, power, and being are conceptual, whereas the Trinity involves real relational distinctions within God.
This directly states how divine simplicity identifies attributes with God's being while preserving the real relational distinctions required by Trinitarian doctrine.
Chris answers a question about whether divine love and power are identical with being, distinguishing conceptual absolute attributes from real relational Trinitarian distinctions.
A truthmaker account can preserve divine simplicity by treating God himself as the single truthmaker for many distinct true predications about God.
The account presents a substantive model for reconciling diverse divine predications with one simple divine reality, directly bearing on the coherence of simplicity.
After concurring with much of Chris's answer, Joe introduces the truthmaker model, distinguishes predicables from properties, and identifies God as their one truthmaker.
God can know what it is like to be a sinner through causal knowledge and empathy without acquiring that knowledge by personally being sinful.
The answer directly addresses whether divine omniscience can encompass creaturely experience without compromising God's moral perfection or requiring creaturely modes of cognition.
In response to an audience question about omniscience and sin, the speaker distinguishes knowing an experience from undergoing it and grounds divine experiential knowledge causally.
Divine impassibility creates pressure against describing God as developing empathy in response to sinners because such responsiveness would imply external influence.
The observation connects simplicity's alleged entailment of impassibility to a potential conflict between divine immutability and responsive empathy toward creatures.
The preceding claim that God's empathy for sinners motivates incarnation and redemption.
After Chris's account of divine empathy and knowledge of sin, Joe flags an impassibility-based objection concerning whether creatures can affect or move God.
Disputes about divine simplicity largely derive from more fundamental disagreements about metaphysics, including essence, existence, accidents, and composition.
This methodological claim identifies the deeper premises governing the debate and explains why conclusions about composition in God depend on prior metaphysical judgments.
While answering a request for introductory resources, Chris argues that readers should first settle basic philosophy of nature and metaphysics before evaluating simplicity.
Trinitarian relations do not presuppose independently constituted divine persons because the persons themselves are identical with their subsistent relations.
The move directly defends the coherence of divine simplicity with Trinitarian distinction by denying that relations introduce prior relata as intrinsic divine parts.
The audience challenge that relations among three divine persons seem to require distinct relata incompatible with simplicity.
Chris answers the Trinitarian compatibility objection by treating personal relations as constitutive of the persons rather than as additional features relating antecedent persons.
The proposed Thomistic account does not make subsistent Trinitarian relations possible under divine simplicity.
This concise rejection preserves the critic's central contention that the classical account has not reconciled real Trinitarian personal distinction with divine simplicity.
Chris's account identifying the divine persons with subsistent relations rather than presupposing persons as separate relata.
Joe declines to supplement Chris's explanation because he continues to regard the requested reconciliation of the Trinity and divine simplicity as impossible.
Extrinsic changes do not temporalize God because the relevant changing relations inhere in creatures, while creatures conform to God's knowledge rather than altering it.
The answer directly addresses the alleged conflict between simplicity, timelessness, and knowledge of changing contingent reality by locating relational change wholly in creatures.
The challenge that extrinsic relational changes involving God would suffice to make God temporal and internally changeable.
Chris distinguishes a creature's changing relation to God from any changing relation inhering in God and supports this through the divine direction of fit.
Many apparent theological disputes about divine simplicity can be evaluated only after clarifying the underlying metaphysics and philosophy of nature.
The closing claim explains how disputes over simplicity should be adjudicated and locates disagreements about the doctrine in more basic philosophical commitments.
In his closing remarks, Chris argues that theological controversies often conceal philosophical disagreements and urges mastery of background metaphysics before judging simplicity.
